judgement.question: The architect asked whether holding the role's handover guard for the whole of TestRoleHolderStateIsNamedByEachRoutesAnswer is right, and whether a handover can release a lapsed claim while a route still answers about it as held — that is, whether a client could see a wrong answer.
judgement.answer: The guard-hold is right, and no client can see a wrong answer. The interleaving is real: a keep starts a handover in a goroutine and that handover resolves the role's holder, which releases a lapsed claim, while the routes answer about the same role.
judgement.measured: On the real stack, 12 rounds of one publish racing a burst of 8 lookups of a role whose holder had claimed it and then had its registration deleted (the e2e rig's lapsed claim). First attempt measured nothing, and I say so because it is the trap: I polled with lookups while waiting for the claim to lapse, and a LOOKUP RELEASES A LAPSED CLAIM TOO, so every answer read `unclaimed` and the race never happened. With the poll removed the race is genuine: 3 of 12 publishes saw `holder_lapsed` naming ses_r8_race and 9 saw `unclaimed`; of 96 lookups, 9 answered 404 holder_lapsed with claim_released true and 87 answered 404 unclaimed.
judgement.theDecidingNumbers: 0 of 96 lookups answered 200, so no route ever named the lapsed holder as live, before or after the release. 12 of 12 publishes answered 202 kept, so no message was lost to the race whichever side won.
judgement.soWhat: The only thing the race decides is WHICH of two truthful 404 reasons a client sees — holder_lapsed with claim_released true if it got there before the release, unclaimed if after — and each answer is true of the moment the request resolved it. That is nondeterminism in the reported reason, not a wrong answer. The test is about the reason each route names, so without the guard the background handover would flip that reason underneath it: the hold removes a flake, it does not mask a defect. I would have reported it as masking one if any lookup had answered 200.
